# Modernization

A discipline module — owns migration method, not the syntax of either
the legacy or the target stack. Combine with whichever stack
conventions skill(s) match the source and target — they ship into a
repo as `.claude/skills/<id>/SKILL.md` and `.cursor/rules/<id>.mdc`,
and only for the stacks that repo uses.

## Name the forcing function before anything else

A migration plan is a risk-management document first and a scope
document second, and the first question it answers is **why now**.

- The reason is a **concrete forcing function with a source and a
  date**: an end-of-life date for the version or the platform, a
  specific security exposure, a cost the current path incurs, or an
  incompatibility that blocks something already committed to.
- **"We should modernize this" is not a reason.** Neither is "it's
  old", "nobody understands it", or "the new one is better". Those may
  all be true and none of them tells anyone when this has to be done by,
  which is the thing every sequencing decision below depends on.
- **An unclear why means the plan isn't ready** — it is not a gap to
  paper over with a general modernization narrative. Say the forcing
  function is `[PENDING]` and ask; a migration nobody can date is a
  migration that will be paused halfway and left there, which is the
  worst of all the available outcomes.
- Never invent a forcing function. An EOL date that turns out to be
  wrong sets the whole sequence to the wrong deadline.

Say alongside it what changes if this goes well — for users, for the
systems that depend on this one, for the teams that operate it — and
what is at risk if it goes badly. Cutover risk is the point of the
document.

## Stage it, don't rewrite it in one shot

- Prefer the strangler-fig pattern: put a routing layer in front of the
  legacy system, migrate one capability at a time behind it, only
  retire the legacy path once every capability routed through it is
  gone
- A big-bang rewrite means the legacy system and the new one diverge
  in behavior for months with no way to compare them — avoid it unless
  the legacy system is small enough that staging genuinely adds no
  value

## Parity before cutover

- Define what "parity" means for this migration up front — functional
  behavior, performance envelope, and data consistency are usually all
  three required, not just the first
- Dark-launch or shadow-traffic the new path against the old one in
  production before routing real users to it — compare outputs, don't
  assume the new implementation is correct because it passed tests
  written against the same assumptions as the code
- A migration isn't verified by "the new system starts up" — it's
  verified by the new system producing the same outcomes as the old
  one on real traffic, for long enough to catch the cases tests missed

## Rollback

- The rollback plan is written and tested *before* cutover, not
  improvised after something breaks — if reverting a cutover isn't a
  known, rehearsed action, the cutover isn't ready
- Keep the legacy path retirable-but-present until parity is confirmed
  in production, not deleted at first sign the new path works
- **Name the point of no return explicitly, as its own statement** — the
  step after which rolling back stops being possible: a destructive
  schema change, a backfill that overwrites the source, an external
  party already notified, a decommissioned dependency. Don't leave it
  inside a general list of risks, where it reads as one concern among
  several rather than as the moment the plan stops having an undo
- If there genuinely isn't one, say "no point of no return" out loud.
  The sentence is what tells the next reader it was considered rather
  than missed
- Everything before that point is reversible and should be sequenced to
  stay that way for as long as possible — the later the irreversible
  step falls in the sequence, the more of the migration gets validated
  under real traffic while retreat is still available

## Migration is done when the old path is deleted

- A migration that leaves both systems running indefinitely "just in
  case" isn't finished — it's a second system to maintain forever,
  and it will quietly rot
- Set a deletion date for the legacy path as part of the migration
  plan, not as an afterthought once things feel stable
